snapshots.title: Claude's recommended dev workflow
snapshots.subtitle: The skills Claude would want loaded across a code project from kickoff to production! Start with Common; layer specialised tracks (Backend / Frontend / Mobile / Data·ML) on top when they apply!
snapshots.note: Each pick cites an exemplar from the corpus when one exists. Click it to read the actual skill.

tracks.name: Common
tracks.tagline: Works for any code project. The baseline every track inherits.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Sharpen a vague idea into a concrete requirements doc and a working scaffold. Most rework comes from skipping this step.

picks.why: Forces you to articulate constraints, non-goals, and 'when NOT to use it' before any code. Saves hours of mid-implementation pivots.

picks.concept: Codebase audit (when joining an existing project)
picks.why: Maps the landscape — modules, hot spots, conventions — before you touch anything. Prevents naive edits that violate hidden invariants.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: Decompose the work, lock down architecture, write the decisions you'll regret forgetting later.

picks.why: PRD → design review → tech decisions → research → metrics. Each gate forces clarity before the next. Half the bugs are killed before they exist.
Scores the design against principles like 'action parity' and 'tools as primitives'. Catches anti-patterns before they're load-bearing.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Small loops, deterministic outputs, frequent checkpoints. Trust the spec from the plan phase.

picks.why: Translates the plan into concrete, ordered steps: worktree isolation, TDD scaffolding, level-based parallel agents, quality-gate smoke tests, PR creation through merge. Subsumes the lighter 'compound work cycle' pattern by adding explicit checkpoints between phases.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Correctness, performance, and security before anything ships. Reviews catch what tests can't.

picks.why: Looks at correctness bugs AND reuse / simplification / efficiency in one pass. Faster than waiting for a human review round-trip.
Hits the user-facing flow after each meaningful change. Catches integration regressions that unit tests miss by design.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Clean up, document, announce. The work isn't done until someone else can use it.

picks.why: Prunes stale branches and clarifies what's in flight. A clean repo is faster to navigate the next morning.
Markdown + Mermaid for architecture, flows, decision trees. Future-you and your teammates will thank present-you.
GIF / terminal recording / screenshots showing the change actually works. Reviewers grok intent in 5 seconds vs reading 500 lines.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Production starts on deploy. Watch the signals you said you'd watch.

picks.why: Tails the relevant dashboards and alerts for N minutes after deploy. Catches the regression while you still remember what changed.
Periodically summarizes what users experienced, how the product performed, and which signals deserve a closer look. Stops bugs from compounding silently.

tracks.name: Backend
tracks.note: Read Common first. These layer on server-side specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Decide language, framework, and deployment target explicitly before any code. These choices shape every later phase.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: API and data model first. Decide write paths and the consistency story before any controller code.

picks.why: Define OpenAPI / gRPC proto / SDL schema before writing handlers. Server and client codegen plus contract tests all build on this single source.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Migrations and request validation are where production tends to break first. Be strict.

picks.why: Additive-only migrations (add column → backfill → switch reads → remove old). Every migration must have a rollback path. Never DROP in the same release as the read switch.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Beyond unit tests, exercise the API the way real clients will.

picks.why: k6 / Locust / wrk against staging with a realistic traffic shape. Measure p95/p99 latency, tail behaviour, and connection-pool exhaustion before production traffic hits.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Servers run 24/7. Observability is not a launch checklist item; it is the operational primitive.

picks.why: JSON logs with request_id plus OpenTelemetry spans across services. Without them, root-causing a production incident is effectively guessing.

tracks.name: Frontend
tracks.note: Read Common first. These layer on frontend specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Audit what already exists in the design system. Don't reinvent buttons.

picks.why: List every existing token, primitive, and pattern before creating new ones. 80% of 'new components' should be assemblies of existing primitives.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: Wireframes precede pixel-perfect designs precede code. Skipping a layer makes the next one painful.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Build in isolation, integrate last. Storybook is leverage.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Pixels matter, accessibility matters, performance matters. Automate each.

picks.why: axe / pa11y in CI + manual keyboard / screen reader pass before launch. Roughly 15% of users benefit; 100% of code reviews should require it.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Don't ship 5MB of JavaScript for a button.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Users hit weird browser versions, weird network conditions, weird input devices. See it from their side.

tracks.name: Mobile
tracks.note: Read Common first. Mobile adds device + store specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Mobile work has high day-0 friction: store accounts, certificates, and platform priority. Resolve these before writing the first screen.

picks.why: iOS-first / Android-first / parity carries real cost implications. Most indie launches pick one and iterate; enterprise typically needs parity. Decide explicitly with a written rationale.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: The cross-platform decision is one of the most expensive choices to reverse. Make it explicit and document why.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: A tight build/simulate loop matters more on mobile. The IDE-to-simulator round-trip dominates iteration time.

picks.why: One command to build, boot the simulator, install, launch, and tail logs. Removes the 30-second context switch on every iteration.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Behavior must hold across a wide range of devices and OS versions, not just the developer's primary device.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Store review rejections come for many reasons. Prepare for them in advance.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Mobile users update slowly; old versions linger in production for months.

tracks.name: Data / ML
tracks.tagline: Data pipelines, model training, scientific computing.
tracks.note: Read Common first. Data / ML adds eval-set discipline and reproducibility.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Look at the data before assuming anything.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: The evaluation set is the project's truth. Build it before any model.

picks.why: Held-out test set + slices for sub-populations + the dumb-baseline number. If you can't articulate the metric and how it's measured, you're not ready to train.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Notebooks are great for exploration, bad for production. Convert at the right moment.

picks.why: K-Dense-AI's collection covers most common ground (zarr for chunked arrays, geomaster for geospatial, fluidsim for CFD, etc.). Reuse before reinventing.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Models lie smoothly. Compare against baselines, watch for drift.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Models without provenance can't be reproduced, can't be audited.

picks.why: Pipeline diagrams (data → features → model → output) make a system reviewable. Mermaid is enough; you don't need draw.io.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Inference cost and latency are now business metrics.

picks.why: Tokens per request, p95/p99 latency, cost per query. Especially with LLM-backed features, cost can spike from a single prompt regression.

tracks.name: Security
tracks.tagline: Cross-cutting concerns: threat model, secrets, dependencies, audit. Apply alongside whichever other track fits the project.
tracks.note: Security touches every phase of every project. Read Common first; treat this track as the security overlay on top.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Identify what you're protecting and from whom before any architecture decision. Threat models built after the fact are theatre.

picks.why: Map trust boundaries, data flows, and threat actors. Ninety minutes here prevents weeks of retrofitted patches. STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is a good starting checklist.
Identify whether PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR, SOC2, or any industry-specific regulation applies. Data residency, retention, audit logging, and encryption defaults all follow from this scope.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: Authentication and data-protection design happen at planning time. These decisions are expensive to reverse mid-build.

picks.why: Sessions vs JWT vs OAuth vs SAML; RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC. Decide the model and where session state lives before the first login screen. Swapping mid-project breaks everything that touched auth.

Classify every data type as public, internal, PII, or secret. Per class, define encryption at rest, encryption in transit, retention period, and access roles. The matrix drives schema, storage, and access-control decisions.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Secrets out of the repository, dependencies under scrutiny, every input validated. The boring foundations.

picks.why: Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Doppler. Never commit credentials to git, never echo them in logs. Rotate on a schedule. Prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived API keys where possible.
Dependabot / Snyk / pip-audit / npm audit / cargo audit in CI. Block PRs introducing known CVEs. Pin transitive dependencies to known-good versions.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Multiple complementary checks: static, dynamic, and human review. No single tool catches everything.

picks.why: A scored posture assessment across authn, authz, data handling, dependency hygiene, and infrastructure. Run on every release candidate.

Focused review against injection, broken access control, identification failures, security misconfiguration, and the rest of the OWASP Top 10. Faster than a full audit; catches the most common classes.
Quick scan of the configuration surface against known threats: leaked tokens, weak defaults, overly permissive CORS, exposed admin endpoints. Run in CI on config changes.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Provenance and integrity of what you ship. Downstream consumers must be able to verify the artifact is the one you built.

picks.why: Sigstore / cosign / GPG-signed releases. Downstream consumers verify the binary they received was actually built by your CI. Critical for supply-chain integrity.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Security is a continuous practice, not a launch milestone. Observe, rotate, respond.

picks.why: Capture authentication events, privileged actions, and data access. Append-only, tamper-evident storage. Retention aligned with compliance scope. Searchable during incident response.
Documented procedure: who to page, how to communicate internally and externally, how to scope blast radius, how to rotate credentials. Tabletop-exercise it quarterly.
Track relevant CVE feeds, vendor advisories, and AI-agent-specific threat patterns. Translate alerts into action items rather than reading them passively.

tracks.name: Backend
tracks.note: Read Common first. These layer on server-side specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Decide language, framework, and deployment target explicitly before any code. These choices shape every later phase.

picks.why: Node / Python / Go / Java / Rust each carry different tradeoffs in team skills, latency profile, deployment story, and ecosystem maturity for your domain. Pick deliberately and capture the reasoning in an ADR.
Serverless vs containers vs VMs vs managed PaaS determines CI shape, observability tooling, scaling story, and cost model. Decide before writing the Dockerfile or serverless.yml.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: API and data model first. Decide write paths and the consistency story before any controller code.

picks.why: Define OpenAPI / gRPC proto / SDL schema before writing handlers. Server and client codegen plus contract tests all build on this single source.
Tables, relationships, indexes — and most importantly access patterns — drawn out before any migration runs. Prevents expensive late-stage rewrites.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Migrations and request validation are where production tends to break first. Be strict.

picks.why: Additive-only migrations (add column → backfill → switch reads → remove old). Every migration must have a rollback path. Never DROP in the same release as the read switch.
Schema-validate every inbound request (Zod / Pydantic / proto). Reject early with clear errors instead of letting bad data leak into the persistence layer.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Beyond unit tests, exercise the API the way real clients will.

picks.why: k6 / Locust / wrk against staging with a realistic traffic shape. Measure p95/p99 latency, tail behaviour, and connection-pool exhaustion before production traffic hits.
Diff the actual implementation against the API contract on every PR. Catches breaking changes before clients see them.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Servers run 24/7. Observability is not a launch checklist item; it is the operational primitive.

picks.why: JSON logs with request_id plus OpenTelemetry spans across services. Without them, root-causing a production incident is effectively guessing.
Separate user-visible errors from internal noise. Burn-rate alerts on the SLO surface real problems and silence background flakes.

tracks.name: Frontend
tracks.note: Read Common first. These layer on frontend specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Audit what already exists in the design system. Don't reinvent buttons.

picks.why: List every existing token, primitive, and pattern before creating new ones. 80% of 'new components' should be assemblies of existing primitives.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: Wireframes precede pixel-perfect designs precede code. Skipping a layer makes the next one painful.

picks.why: Clickable, low-fidelity prototype before any component code. Faster to throw away when the UX is wrong.
Props, slots, controlled vs uncontrolled — sketched on paper before TypeScript. Sane defaults > more options.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Build in isolation, integrate last. Storybook is leverage.

picks.why: Develop each component against its stories, not by tabbing to the live app. Smaller feedback loop = faster iteration.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Pixels matter, accessibility matters, performance matters. Automate each.

picks.why: Snapshot diff (Percy / Chromatic / Playwright) catches the 'we accidentally broke the header on mobile' bug before users do.
axe / pa11y in CI + manual keyboard / screen reader pass before launch. Roughly 15% of users benefit; 100% of code reviews should require it.
Same Playwright/Cypress suite from Common; for frontend work this is where most regressions surface.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Don't ship 5MB of JavaScript for a button.

picks.why: Track bundle size budget per route. Lighthouse perf/a11y/SEO scores in CI. Regressions blocked at PR time.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Users hit weird browser versions, weird network conditions, weird input devices. See it from their side.

picks.why: Sentry / LogRocket capturing JS errors + session replay. Source maps uploaded so stacks are readable. Cumulative Layout Shift alerts too.
RUM (real user monitoring) for LCP, INP, CLS by route. Lab numbers can mislead; real-user p75s are the source of truth.

tracks.name: Mobile
tracks.note: Read Common first. Mobile adds device + store specifics.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Mobile work has high day-0 friction: store accounts, certificates, and platform priority. Resolve these before writing the first screen.

picks.why: iOS-first / Android-first / parity carries real cost implications. Most indie launches pick one and iterate; enterprise typically needs parity. Decide explicitly with a written rationale.

Apple Developer ($99/yr) + Google Play Console ($25 one-time), signing certificates, provisioning profiles, push notification certs. Many teams discover these are missing at submission time, which delays launch by days.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: The cross-platform decision is one of the most expensive choices to reverse. Make it explicit and document why.

picks.why: Write an ADR. Key constraints: team skills, performance ceiling, OS-specific features needed, time-to-market. Avoid drifting into one approach by momentum.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: A tight build/simulate loop matters more on mobile. The IDE-to-simulator round-trip dominates iteration time.

picks.why: One command to build, boot the simulator, install, launch, and tail logs. Removes the 30-second context switch on every iteration.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Behavior must hold across a wide range of devices and OS versions, not just the developer's primary device.

picks.why: iPhone SE through iPhone Pro Max, Pixel 4a through Galaxy S24, OS N-2 through N. Cloud device farms (BrowserStack / Sauce) for breadth; physical devices for touch feel.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Store review rejections come for many reasons. Prepare for them in advance.

picks.why: Privacy manifest, permission justifications, age rating, screenshots for every device class, release notes, what's-new copy. Treat the checklist as a deploy artifact.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Mobile users update slowly; old versions linger in production for months.

picks.why: Crash-free rate per app version. Funnel analytics for critical user paths. A forced-update gate for unfixable older versions.

tracks.name: Data / ML
tracks.tagline: Data pipelines, model training, scientific computing.
tracks.note: Read Common first. Data / ML adds eval-set discipline and reproducibility.

phases.name: 1. Kick off
phases.summary: Look at the data before assuming anything.

picks.why: Read the actual schema, sample rows, distributions. Nulls, encoding, time-zone bugs, label imbalance — these become 80% of project pain if found late.

phases.name: 2. Plan
phases.summary: The evaluation set is the project's truth. Build it before any model.

picks.why: Held-out test set + slices for sub-populations + the dumb-baseline number. If you can't articulate the metric and how it's measured, you're not ready to train.

phases.name: 3. Build
phases.summary: Notebooks are great for exploration, bad for production. Convert at the right moment.

picks.why: Once a notebook 'works', extract into a script with locked seeds, pinned deps, deterministic outputs. The notebook stays for exploration; the script is what runs in CI.
K-Dense-AI's collection covers most common ground (zarr for chunked arrays, geomaster for geospatial, fluidsim for CFD, etc.). Reuse before reinventing.

phases.name: 4. Verify
phases.summary: Models lie smoothly. Compare against baselines, watch for drift.

picks.why: Random / most-frequent-class / last-value-carried-forward — your model must beat the dumb baseline on every metric and slice. If it doesn't, you have a bug.
Compare train vs prod feature distributions periodically. PSI / KL-divergence alerts on the inputs catch silent degradation before metrics tank.

phases.name: 5. Ship
phases.summary: Models without provenance can't be reproduced, can't be audited.

picks.why: What was trained on what data, with what splits, evaluated how, with which limitations. Future-you and your auditors both need this.
Pipeline diagrams (data → features → model → output) make a system reviewable. Mermaid is enough; you don't need draw.io.

phases.name: 6. Operate
phases.summary: Inference cost and latency are now business metrics.

picks.why: Tokens per request, p95/p99 latency, cost per query. Especially with LLM-backed features, cost can spike from a single prompt regression.
